title: Vayeshev: the empty pit (Genesis 37:24)
hookLine: "the pit was empty, there was no water in it"

lines: THE COAT, SEEN FROM FAR OFF.
cards: Some moments in life are just a hole. A diagnosis. A layoff.

The night the house goes quiet after a divorce. You're at the bottom of something, and you can't see a way up. Joseph walks toward his brothers across the fields at Dothan, wearing the coat his father gave him.
They see him coming from far off. Before he reaches them, they've already made a plan.

teach.b: Here comes the dreamer, they say.
Let's kill him, throw him into one of the pits, and say a wild animal ate him. Then we'll see what becomes of his dreams. Reuben, the oldest, steps in.
Don't take his life. Throw him into this pit, here in the wilderness, but don't lay a hand on him. The Torah tells us why: Reuben meant to come back later and rescue him.

So Joseph arrives, and they strip off his coat, the coat, and throw him into the pit. Then one flat detail, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and the pit was empty, there was no water in it."
Why tell us that? If it's empty, of course there's no water. The rabbis read the doubled phrase slowly.

teach.h: NO WATER, BUT SNAKES AND SCORPIONS.
teach.b: The Talmud says: there was no water in it, but there were snakes and scorpions. Empty of what helps, and not empty of what harms. Others hear it more plainly.
It was a cistern for catching rain, and it was dry, so Joseph wouldn't drown. Empty can be terrible. It can also be the thing that keeps you alive.
Then the next verse, flat and cold: the brothers sat down to eat bread.
Their brother is in a hole nearby, and they have lunch. The story doesn't let us look away from that. Joseph is in the pit, stripped, alone, nothing in it but darkness.
And, the story will show, it isn't the end of him.

how: The sale of Joseph is read in synagogues each winter in Vayeshev, and later Jewish tradition links the brothers' sin to the martyrdom of ten sages remembered on Yom Kippur.

o: and he stripped, for the coat taken off
and he settled, though Joseph lands in a pit
and he fell, for Joseph thrown in the pit

games.q: who did what at Dothan — tap the pairs.

s: he talked them out of killing him and meant to come back and rescue him.
the rabbis read 'no water' as meaning snakes and scorpions were there
empty of water, the Talmud says, but not of snakes and scorpions.
after the pit, the brothers sat down to eat
the next verse: they sat down to eat bread.

games.q: your brothers want to kill Joseph. you're Reuben, the oldest. what do you say?
o: throw him into a pit, but don't kill him.
games.why: Reuben said, don't take his life, throw him into this pit. he planned to come back and rescue him.

practice: Where is there a dry pit in your life right now: a friendship that went quiet, a hope that ran out, a hole where a person used to be? Don't rush to fill it; just look at it honestly.
Is it only empty, or is there something in there too, fear, or strength you didn't know you had?

wordCard.voice: Vayeshev. And he settled: the portion where Joseph's brothers throw him into a pit with no water in it, and then sit down to eat.

orig.note: Hebrew: a pit, a cistern for rainwater. Joseph's was dry.

carryVoice: Your line: no water in it. One flat line, read slowly. That's day two hundred three.

sources.q: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 22a; Rashi on Genesis 37:24
